notes:
User is planning a large backyard BBQ and wants practical, novice-friendly cooking ideas. Planned menu now includes smoked brisket, ribs, BBQ pulled pork sandwiches with coleslaw and pickles, burgers, hot dogs, and grilled pineapple. A grilled-pineapple idea came from the user’s friend Emily, who brought it to the user’s birthday party.

User recently bought a new Weber gas grill, which they enjoy for quick weeknight dinners. It can also be used for burgers, hot dogs, and pineapple, though low-and-slow brisket or pulled pork requires suitable smoker equipment or modifications.

BBQ sauce preference has changed: Kansas City Masterpiece is currently their favorite and planned for ribs and pulled pork. They are open to trying alternatives. Previously they had loved Sweet Baby Ray’s and macaroni and cheese; continue to acknowledge these preferences, but do not describe Sweet Baby Ray’s as the current favorite. Possible sauce suggestions include Sweet Baby Ray’s, Franklin, Stubb’s, Bone Suckin’, or Dinosaur Bar-B-Q, matched to preferred sweet, tangy, smoky, or spicy profiles. Consider offering several sauces for guests.

Their brisket plan is a whole 10–12 lb brisket, trimmed of excess fat and silver skin, seasoned with Killer Hogs BBQ Rub, smoked low and slow around 225°F using post oak, and served with barbecue sauce as desired. Emphasize clean/stable smoker setup, airflow, optional water pan, and a smoker box or foil pouch for chips rather than chips directly on coals. Explain wrapping as a flexible step used when the brisket reaches an appropriate temperature/color, generally around 160–170°F internal, then monitor probe tenderness. Avoid presenting 160°F as merely a food-safety endpoint; brisket usually needs much higher temperatures before shredding, often around 195–205°F depending on cut. Rest before slicing.

Pulled pork will be served on a bun with coleslaw and pickles. Recommend a boneless pork shoulder or Boston butt in a realistic larger size (roughly 8–12 lb for a party), seasoned ahead, smoked around 225–250°F, using mild fruit wood such as apple or cherry, or hickory/pecan sparingly. Cook largely to probe tenderness, often around 195–205°F, then rest and shred. Do not rely on a universal 8–10-hour time.

Grilled pineapple should use a ripe but firm pineapple, such as Smooth Cayenne; core and cut into rings or wedges, oil lightly, and grill over medium-high heat with minimal handling until caramelized and lightly charred. It can be seasoned simply with salt, brown sugar, or cinnamon. Good burger/hot-dog ideas include caramelized onions, bacon, grilled pineapple, specialty cheeses, pickled jalapeños, international-inspired condiments, chili-cheese dogs, Chicago-style dogs, bacon jam, spicy mustard, and chili-lime aioli. Follow current USDA food-safety guidance rather than repeating outdated temperatures; burgers and sausages should be cooked to their recommended safe internal temperature.

Sides suggested or relevant include a tangy coleslaw to cut brisket’s richness, baked beans, grilled vegetables, cornbread, macaroni and cheese, potato salad, collard greens, hush puppies, fried okra, cucumber salad, fruit salad, garlic bread, roasted sweet potatoes, and green salad. User especially loves macaroni and cheese.

Keep explanations clear, practical, enthusiastic, and safety-conscious. Correct prior misinformation if needed, especially fixed cook times, undersized pork portions, and treating 160°F as the target temperature for brisket.
